question: An 8-year-old boy presents to your office for a routine well-child visit. Upon physical examination, he is found to have a harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur that is best appreciated at the left sternal border. The murmur becomes louder when you ask him to make fists with his hands. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur at left sternal border" -> "Murmur louder with fist clenching" -> "Increased systemic vascular resistance" -> "Increased left ventricular pressure" -> "Ventricular septal defect" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur at left sternal border" -> "Murmur louder with fist clenching" -> "Increased afterload on the left ventricle" -> "Left ventricular hypertrophy" -> 70%
analysis: The harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur that increases in intensity with hand grip maneuvers is characteristic of a ventricular septal defect (VSD). This defect allows blood to flow from the left ventricle to the right ventricle during systole, causing the murmur. The location of the murmur at the left sternal border is also typical for a VSD.
